extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, PR managers, editors and designers preparing brochures, fact sheets, newsletters, newspapers, and magazines
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for planning, designing, producing, and evaluating brochures, fact sheets, direct mail, newsletters, newspapers, and magazines used in public relations. Covers format selection, layout, typography, printing, working with printers, audience targeting, and evaluation techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel positioning and use (brochure panels)
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle panel of the same side of the sheet becomes the 'back' side and occupies the least advantageous position; it may be used for supplementary information or left blank except for a return-address section so the brochure can be mailed without an envelope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide how the three panels on the reverse side will read (single poster spread; left-hand single page + two-panel spread; or three separate panels left-to-right) depending on amount of information, personality of design, and whether information should be presented linearly or randomly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format selection for cost and familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: When the object is to keep the cost down (between five and fifteen cents per brochure) and present a familiar artifact, standard two- and three-fold formats work best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard 8½ x 11 sheet fold formats for economical mailings; consider nonstandard formats only if budget allows and to intrigue reader or achieve a lavish feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium appropriateness: controlled media advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Brochures, fact sheets, and direct mail are 'controlled' media: the practitioner does not have to tailor the message to pass gatekeepers of news media and can write what they want and put it directly in readers' hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of control, select objectives like retention and exposure; expect effect on cognitions and sometimes attitudes and behaviors when items reach aware or active publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience suitability: best for active publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed publications provide an excellent way to get a message to actively communicating, information-seeking publics; they are ineffective for passive publics unless mailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active publics seek out or pick up publications; passive publics seldom take initiative—mailing can reach passive publics but they must exert more effort than listening to radio/TV and may consider it junk mail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-relations model fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Brochures and fact sheets can be used with any of the four PR models, but practitioners of the public-information model use them most; they also have value in two-way asymmetric model and can be used by symmetric practitioners with caveats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetric practitioners should present tentative positions in printed publications sent to adversary publics and be willing to negotiate after response; avoid presenting a brochure claim as the organization's final non-negotiable position to adversaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility for specialized programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Brochures and fact sheets are versatile for specialized PR programs: employee relations benefits, press kits as background for reporters, educational/community tour information, and financial info for stockholders and brokers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select format, tone, and detail level to suit the specialized audience and function (e.g., press kit vs. employee pamphlet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and resource budgeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Brochures and fact sheets must be printed, requiring more cost and time for preparation than press releases or audio tapes, but are less costly than videotapes, magazines, or newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget money and preparation time; preparation won't overtax resources but requires planning and cost/benefit decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation: readability and behavioral measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Brochures and fact sheets are subject to evaluation using readability formulas or the signaled stopping technique; measure retention, acceptance, and effects on attitudes and behavior using methods described in the evaluation chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use readership studies, signaled stopping, and retention/acceptance measures to determine if the publication fits the target public and achieves communication objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-cover placement for rack display
rubrics_metrics.description: If disseminated from a rack or holder sharing space with similar messages, the front cover must be arranged with title or 'teaser' on the top third of the front panel so it can be seen peeking out over competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the cover should be unique, it must stylistically relate to remaining panels through consistent typography and art materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing copy for multipanel layouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Write copy so it forms a complete linear message, then divide it into suitable segments for each panel; key sentences should be highlighted by display type instead of regular text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep presentation balanced (approx same number of titles/headlines per panel) or use a multipanel overline to hold text together; ensure each panel 'pulls' the reader to the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting and placing art
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide between several small pieces of art or a single picture that will carry the entire message depending on number of appeals/examples provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for emotional appeal, place a reversed startling statistic (light lettering over dark image) over a photo; ensure art supports the message and consider halftone needs for photographs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupon design and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: If including a coupon, ideally place it on a separate slip so the main message is not mutilated when coupon is removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If coupon must be torn from the brochure due to budget, put it on the flap farthest from the cover and ensure no important information is removed when torn; echo type, art, and slogan of main brochure on the insert for stylistic relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sideways reading and mixed orientations
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist designing a brochure to read sideways (8½-inch measure as width, pages flipped from bottom); do not mix horizontal and vertical makeup if you want reader to complete multipanel layout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sideways layouts useful only for wide statistical tables; mixing orientations is usually perceived as odd and annoying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title handling on cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not tilt the main title ninety degrees unless it is one or two simple, easy-to-recognize words; complex titles should be run in orthodox fashion, at most tipped up to thirty degrees if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep cover wording clear and legible; bold confrontational super-sized type can be effective if appropriate to message ('The five minutes you spend reading this pamphlet could save your life!').

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover composition balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The cover is most effective when approximately one-third type and two-thirds illustration or visual relief (white space); occasionally impact is achieved by totally filling cover with super-sized type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain stylistic relation across panels; ensure cover either intrigues or clearly labels the topic and begins development of concept supported inside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel-to-panel continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some element on each panel should 'pull' the reader on from the previous panel (illustration, headline, boxed item, statistical table, or layout variation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading an all-text message is hard work; provide incentives to continue such as bold headlines, boxed items, or visual elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive for visual equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: A brochure should not be top-heavy, bottom-heavy, right- or left-heavy, front-loaded, or crammed at the back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If copy equals three pages of text, use white space and wider margins to spread it evenly; avoid dumping gratuitous art at the end to fill space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish family resemblance across publications
rubrics_metrics.description: If part of a 'family' of messages, use devices that make the family resemblance obvious: organization logo and slogan, distinctive color or border devices, and familiar typefaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency helps recognition and branding across multiple publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use boxed/bordered items for longevity and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Liven presentation with boxed or bordered items such as maps, directions, 'how-to' explanations, and lists; inclusion of vital information assures longevity as recipients may need it later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question-and-answer format is a durable, simple, and recognizable way to draw reader in; write Q lines in larger/bolder type and pose intriguing 'What if?' or 'How come?' questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question-and-answer format guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Q-and-A format draws the reader in and is effective when Q lines appear in larger or bolder type and the questions are intriguing and punchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loaded or petty questions that alienate readers (example anti-pattern: 'Why don't the conservatives care about the little man?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spot color with restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Spot color will dress up a brochure but should not be splotched around with wild abandon; restraint and good taste are preferable to gratuitous excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try a single dark ink with a contrasting color title, or back one panel with a halftone screen; when in doubt, review printer's past examples to judge quality look.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working with printers: plan and provide samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring rough layouts or samples of similar jobs to the printer; avoid coming with the job so firmly worked out that you're totally inflexible as that may increase costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact three or four printers well ahead of time; obtain samples of their work; find out what services they handle in-house vs outsource; competitive bids reveal disparities in costs for typesetting, binding, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask for a breakdown bid
rubrics_metrics.description: Request a 'breakdown bid' that indicates how price differs depending on grade of paper, type of ink, number of pictures, copy run, and use of spot color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If budget is limited, trade off items (e.g., better paper but sacrifice second ink); know what drives price so you can make informed choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printer contract checkpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Before signing the printer's contract, check: (1) turnaround time from delivery of copy to receipt of proofs and how long you have to correct and return proofs; (2) how much material you can correct/change without paying extra; (3) delivery location of finished job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out a production schedule that specifies days allocated to each step; clarify correction allowances (some printers allow up to 10% without penalty); if material is to be mailed, consider a printer who can prepare for postal delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn basic printing, typesetting, and reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: A working acquaintance with typography and printing helps you work effectively with printers; learn basics of printing methods, artwork reproduction, typesetting, and type characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take a graphics course or self-study; know printing methods (offset, letterpress, gravure), artwork reproduction differences (line art vs continuous-tone halftones), and typesetting processes (phototypesetting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing methods and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Offset is the predominant method giving a flat even image and inexpensive art reproduction; letterpress gives a sharper, glossier look; gravure is used for large jobs needing high-quality color photo reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose printing method appropriate to job size, budget, and required reproduction quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artwork reproduction rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Line drawings (no intermediate grays) can be reproduced quickly and cheaply; continuous-tone art (photographs) must be converted to halftone screens (dot patterns) for proper inking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for halftone processing and placement of photographs accordingly in layout and budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Most text and display type today is handled through phototypesetting (electronic); some special display types are still set mechanically or by hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phototypesetting produces type strips to be pasted onto layout; be aware of display type options and what the printer can provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typeface personality and family use
rubrics_metrics.description: Every typeface has characteristics (plain, fancy, bold, italic) and a 'personality' (masculine, feminine, humorous, serious); types belong to families with weight and style variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select typefaces consistent with message tone and family variations to provide contrast without inconsistency; consult printer's specimen book for options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layout basic elements and phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Layout consists of four basic elements—body type (text), display type (headlines), art (photos/drawings), and white space. Preparation goes through three phases: rough layout/dummy, comprehensive layout ('comp'), and final production-ready pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use layout sheets with light-blue pencil (invisible in photography) to sketch elements; ensure comp is precise enough for printer to measure exact space for each item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use white space to manage dense copy
rubrics_metrics.description: If copy is too long (equivalent of three pages of text), use white space and wider margins to spread it out evenly rather than cramming or adding gratuitous art to fill space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: White space improves readability and visual balance; avoid overfilling or top/bottom heavy designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select publication format to match content and prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose newspaper tabloid format for many 'hard' news items and inexpensive production; choose slick, heavy-paper magazine format for longer illustrated features and when a durable, prestigious product is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider minimags for quick browseability, maganews hybrids for modern graphics and flexibility, and 8½-by-11 offset newsletters for ease of production and mailing convenience depending on audience and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate print publications with readership studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Because print publications most realistically aim at communication (exposure/retention), readership studies and signaled stopping techniques are usually the most appropriate evaluation techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether audience reads and retains content; if audience is passive, justify expense before committing to production and consider targeted formats to increase engagement.
